title: Abraham Lincoln & Edwin Stanton: Does That Horse Have 'Splints'?
summary: When Secretary of War Stanton admitted approving a confusing, unintelligible military telegram in haste, Lincoln brought down the house with a frontier tale of a boy selling a horse with 'splints'.
keywords: Abraham Lincoln & Edwin Stanton: Does That Horse Have 'Splints'?
full_text:
In 1862, during the American Civil War, President Lincoln and Secretary of War Edwin Stanton were poring over battlefield dispatches.

Stanton confessed: "Mr. President, a hurried telegram arrived from General Mitchell on the front. I could not make heads or tails of what Mitchell was asking. But since military matters cannot wait, I fired off an immediate reply saying: 'All right, go ahead!' If Mitchell was asking to execute a disastrous maneuver, I may have to revoke the order at once!"

Lincoln leaned back in his leather chair, smiling:
"Stanton, your predicament reminds me of a horse-trading boy back in Kentucky.
A farmer came to inspect a horse being sold by a young lad.
The farmer asked: 'Son, does this horse have splints?'
Now, the boy had no earthly idea what 'splints' were! But he wanted to make the sale.
So the lad looked the farmer square in the eye and said: 'Well, mister, if splints are good for a horse, he's got plenty of 'em! But if splints are bad for a horse, he hasn't got a single speck of 'em in his whole body!'"

The staff officers burst into laughter.

Lincoln turned to Stanton:
"Your telegram to General Mitchell is in the exact same condition as that Kentucky horse!
If what Mitchell plans to do is good, your order to 'go ahead' is inspired genius! But if it is disastrous, your order is a catastrophe! Wouldn't it be wiser to find out what a general is asking before telling him to go ahead?"

Stanton grinned, admitting his blunder. Through frontier humor, Lincoln corrected his war secretary without rancor or humiliation.
moral: Great leaders resolve friction and correct subordinates not through authoritarian scolding, but through illuminating humor that exposes logical fallacies with good cheer.
